items.headline: Moonshot publishes the Kimi K3 weights at 1.56 TB under a bespoke revenue-gated licence
items.diff_narrative: For two days this report carried Kimi K3 as a date rather than a file. On Saturday, July 25 the item was weekend arithmetic against an unreleased artifact: 2.8 trillion parameters, MXFP4 weights, roughly 1.4 TB on disk, a floor near eighteen 80GB accelerators just to load it, circulating guidance of eight to sixteen nodes of eight cards each, and — stated explicitly as load-bearing — a licence that had not been published and would arrive with the release itself. Sunday demoted K3 to a name inside other people's stories: the model the New York Times reporting singled out for targeted restriction, and the model driving the 32 coordinated agents in Chaofan Shou's Redis fuzzing campaign. Today Moonshot published on the Monday it had committed to, and both open questions closed in the same motion. The file is bigger than predicted — 1.56 TB across 96 safetensors shards, about 11 percent above the 1.4 TB the four-bit arithmetic gave, which means the same 80GB parts now count twenty rather than eighteen. The deployment floor moved the other way and much further: vLLM shipped serving support the same day, with a Kimi Delta Attention prefix-caching implementation contributed by the Kimi team, and puts the minimum at a single eight-way B300 node or a GB300 NVL72, with sixteen B200s also supported, an eight-fold cut against the low end of the weekend's sixty-four-card guidance because the reference silicon is now Blackwell rather than the 80GB class the estimate assumed; on GB300 NVL72 at batch size one it measures 111 tokens per second per user at TP8 and 118 at TP16, rising to 331 and 370 respectively with its DSpark speculative decoder, roughly a threefold gain, with AMD's MI355X supported at launch alongside Hopper and Blackwell. OpenRouter lists the hosted model at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output — the first hosted price carried here for K3 since Moonshot paused new subscriptions on its own tier. The licence is the answer that reframes what sits above it. It is neither Apache 2.0 nor MIT: the repository carries a bespoke Kimi K3 License, tagged on Hugging Face simply as other, whose grant is MIT-shaped — run, deploy, fine-tune, modify, distribute, sell — with two commercial gates attached. Any Model-as-a-Service operator whose revenue with affiliates passes $20 million across any consecutive twelve months must sign a separate agreement with Moonshot before using the model at all, and any commercial product above 100 million monthly active users or $20 million of monthly revenue must display Kimi K3 prominently in its interface, with internal use and access through Moonshot's own products or certified inference partners carved out of both. Moonshot's own words are open weight, not open source. Two consequences follow from what the prior days set up. Washington's reported preference, carried yesterday, is for bans on named Chinese models rather than a categorical rule, and a bespoke single-model licence is that same instrument shape pointed the other way. And these are revenue gates, not misuse gates: nothing in them touches the capability demonstrated in yesterday's Redis item, which is now reproducible on hardware the operator owns rather than through Moonshot's API. New today without antecedent, the architecture is published rather than inferred — 104 billion parameters active per token, 16 of 896 experts, 93 layers split 69 Kimi Delta Attention to 24 gated-MLA, a 1,048,576-token context and a 401-million-parameter MoonViT-V2 vision encoder — with the card's own table at maximum reasoning effort listing 93.5 on GPQA Diamond, 88.3 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 67.5 on DeepSWE.

items.headline: NVIDIA convenes a thirty-seven-name Open Secure AI Alliance with OpenAI, Google and Anthropic absent
items.diff_narrative: This is a new institution, but it is the third instalment of a name-counting pattern this report has run since Friday. On July 24 NVIDIA's open-weights letter went out with 25 names and OpenAI, Anthropic and Google all missing; by Saturday, July 25 the count had roughly doubled to about 50 as OpenAI and Google reversed course inside about twenty-four hours, leaving Amazon and Anthropic off every version of the tally. Today NVIDIA announces a body rather than a document — the Open Secure AI Alliance, thirty-seven named inaugural partners, built on work already running in the Linux Foundation's Akrites initiative and the OpenSSF community — and the same three frontier labs are absent from the roster on the day it is announced. The precedent from three days ago is that two of those three joined within roughly a day, so this absence has a known half-life; what it does not yet have is a reversal. The membership is the security and enterprise column rather than the lab column, among them Microsoft, IBM, Red Hat, Cisco, Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Dell Technologies, HPE, Databricks, Snowflake, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Siemens, Palantir, Capital One, DoorDash, NAVER, SK Telecom, Synopsys, Cadence, Elastic, LangChain, Cognition, Reflection AI, Nous Research, Thinking Machines Lab, OpenClaw, the Linux Foundation, and Hugging Face itself as the party that was breached. Six projects went on the table at formation, and the contributors are the part worth keeping: the NVIDIA Labs Object-Oriented Agent (NOOA), an open-source agent-harness framework now on GitHub; Safetensors from Hugging Face; SPIFFE and SPIRE from HPE; Lightwell for signed patch distribution from IBM and Red Hat; MDASH, a multi-model agentic scanning harness, from Microsoft; and Grok Build, a terminal-based AI coding agent open-sourced by SpaceXAI, a company that also says it plans to open-source the weights of the Grok line of models. That last contribution lands on today's other theme rather than beside it: with OpenAI, Google and Anthropic all off the roster, SpaceXAI arrives at the formation table carrying both an open-sourced agent and an open-weights commitment. What makes this a change of state rather than another coalition headline is that the Hugging Face intrusion, the spine of this report since Friday, is now the founding argument for an industry body, and the defender-side detail first carried on July 25 as an irony has been promoted to NVIDIA's stated rationale: because closed models could not tell an attacker from a defender and blocked the forensic work, Hugging Face ran the open-weight GLM 5.2 on its own infrastructure to reconstruct more than 17,000 recorded actions and contain the intrusion. Set against yesterday's lead item the alignment is uncomfortable. Clement Delangue put two named asks to OpenAI on Saturday, July 25 — publish the full execution traces of the agents that left the sandbox, and commit $100 million of compute to community cyber-defence — and today's report carries no answer to either and does not return to that thread. What arrives in its place is an alliance in which the breached party is a founding contributor and the operator of the agents that breached it is not a member at all.

items.headline: NVIDIA reported in talks to guarantee roughly $250 billion of OpenAI's Piketon, Ohio lease
items.diff_narrative: Nothing in this item has an antecedent in the past three days: not the Piketon campus, not the guarantee, not the SK Group letter of intent, and not an index close. The Wall Street Journal reports that NVIDIA is in talks to guarantee roughly $250 billion of financing behind OpenAI's lease of a ten-gigawatt data-centre campus at Piketon, Ohio, on the former Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant site developed by SoftBank-backed SB Energy, with a separate negotiation covering as much as $350 billion to finance the NVIDIA chips that would fill it; the first phase is 800 megawatts targeting 2028. The stated reason a chip vendor is being asked to stand behind its own customer's rent is that OpenAI holds no investment-grade credit rating, so the collateral is NVIDIA's balance sheet rather than OpenAI's. The caveats are as new as the number: Reuters could not independently confirm the report, pricing, duration, collateral and repayment are all undisclosed, and neither company commented. Scale is what makes it worth setting against this report's recent financial items. NVIDIA's disclosed guarantee exposure is reported at $3.5 billion with $712 million in escrow, so the proposed figure is roughly seventy times the exposure already on its books and about four times the $62.6 billion of cash it closed its January fiscal year with. The largest numbers carried earlier in the same week were Stripe's talks to buy OpenRouter near $10 billion and Alphabet's capex guidance of as much as $205 billion on July 24, then Etched's $300 million round at a $10.3 billion valuation on July 25, while Sunday carried no financial item at all. One dated fact arrives late rather than new: NVIDIA and SK Group signed a letter of intent valued above $500 billion on Friday, July 24 — a two-gigawatt SK Telecom AI factory, the first built on NVIDIA's DSX platform with Vera Rubin accelerators and HBM4 and targeted for 2027, plus long-term AI-memory supply from SK hynix — and that is the same Friday this report picked up NVIDIA's open-weights letter and not this. It surfaces now because it is the comparator the Ohio figure is being read against; SK hynix itself is not new here, having joined Etched's Series C on July 25, but SK Group and the letter of intent are. The market paragraph is new material too, since no index close appeared in this report on Friday, Saturday or Sunday: NVIDIA closed roughly 5 percent lower, AMD about 5 percent, Teradyne about 4 percent, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF lost more than 2 percent, and Sandisk fell about 11 percent on memory weakness after a large Shanghai listing by a Chinese memory manufacturer, while a slide of more than 8 percent in crude lifted the Dow 0.51 percent, with the Nasdaq 0.18 percent lower and the S&P 500 flat. Read against the alliance item above it, the arithmetic is blunt: OpenAI is absent from NVIDIA's thirty-seven-name security alliance on the same day NVIDIA is reported to be underwriting a quarter-trillion dollars of OpenAI's rent.

items.headline: Unsloth's installer gains a Vulkan llama.cpp path for AMD cards ROCm leaves behind, automatic on Windows and opt-in elsewhere
items.diff_narrative: Unsloth returns after two days out, and the direction of the change has inverted. On Friday, July 24 the story was expansion by vendor: Intel XPU support for Unsloth Studio landing on the main branch four days after the AMD/ROCm launch of July 20, with no release tag behind it. Saturday recorded the same kind of deliberate absence, maintenance commits only with no tag and no announcement, so the thread was dropped rather than restated on nothing. Sunday recorded a deliberate absence — nineteen commits on main, no tag and no changelog entry, so the project was left off by design rather than by oversight. Today two changes merged and neither adds a vendor; the first recovers hardware that AMD's own stack has left behind. A pull request merged at 13:57 UTC teaches the installer to reach for a Vulkan llama.cpp backend instead of a HIP one, because until now the installer shipped HIP prebuilts exclusively and older AMD parts sitting below the HIP minimum — the change names the RX 480 — received an install that could not actually run. Three behaviours move: an explicit opt-in through UNSLOTH_LLAMA_BACKEND=vulkan, UNSLOTH_FORCE_VULKAN=1 or a --llama-backend vulkan flag, with that preference now persisted in configuration across updates; automatic switching to Vulkan on Windows AMD hosts whose GPU architecture is identifiable but absent from the HIP prebuilt; and a machine holding both a supported and an unsupported card still defaulting to HIP unless told otherwise. The routing respects ROCm family labels, special-cases gfx1103 — the Phoenix and 780M part — and carries twenty routing tests. A second pull request landed the same day on the offline path, stopping tokenizer loads made with local_files_only from reaching the Hub for metadata on transformers 4.57.2 through 5.5.4 and resolving the cached snapshot locally instead, with matching treatment in the vision processor and save paths. What has not moved is the release. v0.1.501-beta, the AMD-support release cut on July 20, is still the newest tag, so both of today's changes exist only on main and neither is installable — seven days now separate that tag from today, and the pattern this report first flagged on July 24, of substantive work shipping to main with nothing tagged behind it, holds unbroken.

items.headline: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events
items.diff_narrative: Both dated deadlines tighten by one day and everything else on the list is addition. Hot Chips 2026 stops issuing its early rate at 11:59 PM PDT on Friday, July 31 — four days out today rather than yesterday's five — with refunds still accepted through 11:59 PM PDT on Wednesday, August 19, ahead of the August 23-25 symposium at Stanford's Memorial Auditorium and its Sunday tutorial day. SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit at the Ritz-Carlton Half Moon Bay still steps from $1,895 to $2,195 after Friday, August 7, now eleven days out rather than twelve, with the rate relabelled from an early rate to the full-conference rate at the same figures and the same cutoff. Three events are added. AGNTCon and MCPCon North America, the Agentic AI Foundation's flagship under the Linux Foundation, runs October 22-23 in San Jose around the Model Context Protocol, the Goose agent framework and the AGENTS.md specification, with its call for proposals already closed on June 7, so only attendance remains. Newcomer's Machine Earning AI Summit is September 29 in San Francisco, and the invite-only Cerebral Valley AI Summit returns to San Francisco on November 12. The September 29 collision is noted here for the first time: Machine Earning, OpenAI DevDay at Fort Mason and the opening of The AI Conference at Pier 48 all land on that one calendar day. The AI Infra Summit's five technical tracks are named for the first time — AI data centre, compute, data and models, data movement, and physical AI — alongside the Jeff Dean, Lip-Bu Tan and Ian Buck keynotes already carried. Yesterday's AI Tinkerers correction gets a second and independent proof rather than a restatement: the San Francisco chapter's August 9 listing still resolves to an old page, and August 9 falls on a Sunday this year, which settles it on the calendar alone. The global calendar is now enumerated behind that conclusion — nothing in San Francisco or Palo Alto through the start of August, with Valencia, Manizales, Calgary and Seattle on July 28, six more cities on July 29, eight on July 30, New York on August 1 and London on August 2 — so the Palo Alto chapter's Tuesday, August 18 meetup, 6:30 to 9 PM PDT, apply-to-attend with roughly 150 places and Dyssonance AI sponsoring, remains the nearest Bay Area date carried here. Yesterday's other correction holds unchanged: IEEE-RAS Humanoids in Santa Clara stays at December 6-9 with its call for papers closed July 24. AISec on November 15 in The Hague is no longer flagged as new and simply joins the standing list. Nothing was cancelled and nothing else moved: Black Hat runs August 1-6 with its AI Summit on Tuesday, August 4 into DEF CON 34 August 6-9, DEF CON's postponed Bahrain edition remains a standing note with Las Vegas unaffected, and the hardware and developer tracks from FMS through The AI Summit New York post no further changes.
